The '''quadratic Frobenius test''' ('''QFT''') is a [[Probabilistic algorithm|probabilistic]] [[primality test]] to determine whether a number is a [[probable prime]]. It is named after [[Ferdinand Georg Frobenius]]. The test uses the concepts of [[quadratic polynomial]]s and the [[Frobenius automorphism]]. It should not be confused with the more general [[Frobenius pseudoprime|Frobenius test]] using a quadratic polynomial – the QFT restricts the polynomials allowed based on the input, and also has other conditions that must be met. A [[composite number|composite]] passing this test is a [[Frobenius pseudoprime]], but the converse is not necessarily true.

==Concept==
Grantham's stated goal when developing the algorithm was to provide a test that primes would always pass and composites would pass with a probability of less than 1/7710.<ref name="Grantham">{{cite journal | last = Grantham | first = J. | title = A Probable Prime Test With High Confidence | journal = Journal of Number Theory | volume = 72 | issue = 1 | pages = 32–47 | date = 1998 | doi = 10.1006/jnth.1998.2247 | s2cid = 119640473 | arxiv = 1903.06823 }}</ref>{{rp|33}}

The test was later extended by [[Ivan Damgård|Damgård]] and Frandsen to a test called ''extended quadratic Frobenius test'' (EQFT).<ref name="DamFran">{{cite book | last1 = Damgård | first1 = Ivan Bjerre | authorlink1 = Ivan Damgård | last2 = Frandsen | first2 = Gudmund Skovbjerg  | title = Fundamentals of Computation Theory | chapter = An Extended Quadratic Frobenius Primality Test with Average and Worst Case Error Estimates | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science | year = 2003 | volume = 2751  | pages = 118–131 | publisher = Springer Berlin Heidelberg | isbn = 978-3-540-45077-1 | issn = 1611-3349 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-540-45077-1_12 | url = https://www.brics.dk/RS/03/9/BRICS-RS-03-9.pdf}}</ref>

==Algorithm==
Let {{mvar|n}} be a positive integer such that {{mvar|n}} is odd, and let ''b'' and ''c'' be integers such that <math>\left(\frac{b^2+4c}{n}\right) = -1</math> and <math>\left(\frac{-c}{n}\right) = 1</math>, where <math>\left(\frac{\cdot}{\cdot}\right)</math> denotes the [[Jacobi symbol]]. Set <math>B = 50000</math>. Then a ''QFT'' on {{mvar|n}} with parameters ({{mvar|b}}, {{mvar|c}}) works as follows:

:'''(1)''' Test whether any of the primes less than or equal to <math>\min(B, \sqrt{n})</math> divides {{mvar|n}}. If yes, then stop: {{mvar|n}} is composite.
:'''(2)''' Test whether <math>\sqrt{n} \in \mathbb{Z}</math>. If yes, then stop: {{mvar|n}} is composite.
:'''(3)''' Compute <math>x^{n+1 \over 2}\,\bmod\,\big(n,x^2-bx-c)</math>. If <math>x^{n+1 \over 2} \notin \mathbb{Z} \big / n \mathbb{Z}</math>, then stop: {{mvar|n}} is composite.
:'''(4)''' Compute <math>x^{n+1}\,\bmod\,\big(n,x^2-bx-c)</math>. If <math>x^{n+1} \not\equiv -c</math>, then stop: {{mvar|n}} is composite.
:'''(5)''' Let <math>n^2-1=2^{r}s</math> with {{mvar|s}} odd. If <math>x^s \not\equiv 1 \bmod\,\big(n,x^2-bx-c)</math>, and <math>x^{2^{j}s} \not\equiv -1 \bmod\,\big(n,x^2-bx-c)</math> for all <math>0 \leq j \leq r-2</math>, then stop: {{mvar|n}} is composite.

If the ''QFT'' does not stop in steps (1)–(5), then {{mvar|n}} is a probable prime.

(The notation <math>A \equiv  B \bmod \, (n, \, f(x))</math> means that <math>A - B = H(x) \cdot n + K(x) \cdot f(x)</math>, where H and K are polynomials.)
